tasks.description: Write a decorator `shout` that makes any function's string return value uppercase. Apply it to a function that returns 'hello world'.
tasks.hint:
A decorator is a function that wraps another function.
`def shout(func): def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return func(*args, **kwargs).upper(); return wrapper`
Apply with `@shout` above the function definition.
tasks.walkthrough:
`shout` receives the original function and returns `wrapper`, which calls it and uppercases the result.
`@shout` replaces `greet` with that wrapper, so calling `greet()` now goes through it.

tasks.description: Write a decorator `timer` that prints how long a function takes to run. Apply it to a function that loops 1 million times.
tasks.hint:
`import time` — use `time.time()` before and after calling the function.
`start = time.time(); result = func(*args, **kwargs); end = time.time()`
Print: `print(f'Took {end - start:.4f}s')` then return result.
tasks.walkthrough:
The wrapper notes the time, runs the real function, notes the time again, and prints the difference.
It still returns the function's result, so `print(count())` shows the total after the timing line.

tasks.description: Write a decorator `repeat(n)` that calls a function n times. Apply it so a function prints 'Hello!' three times.
tasks.hint:
This is a decorator FACTORY — it takes an argument.
`def repeat(n): def decorator(func): def wrapper(*a, **kw): [func(*a, **kw) for _ in range(n)]; return wrapper; return decorator`
Apply: `@repeat(3)` above the function.
tasks.walkthrough:
`repeat(3)` is called first and returns `decorator`. That decorator is then applied to `say_hello`.
The innermost wrapper loops `n` times, calling the original each time.

tasks.description: Write a decorator `log_call` that prints 'Calling {func_name}' before a function runs. Test it.
tasks.hint:
Inside the wrapper: `print(f'Calling {func.__name__}')` before calling func.
`func.__name__` gives the function's name as a string.
This is useful for debugging — you can see exactly which functions are being called.
tasks.walkthrough:
`func.__name__` is the original function's name as a string, so the message says which function is being called.
The wrapper then calls it with the same arguments and passes the result back.

tasks.description: Stack two decorators on one function: `@log_call` and `@shout`. Show that both run (prints the call log AND uppercases the output).
tasks.hint:
Decorators stack from bottom up — the closest to the function runs first.
`@log_call` then `@shout` on the next line means: shout wraps the function, then log_call wraps that.
The order can matter — experiment to see the difference.
tasks.walkthrough:
`@shout` is closest to the function so it wraps first; `@log_call` wraps the result of that.
Calling `greet()` runs log_call's wrapper (prints the message), which calls shout's wrapper, which calls the original and uppercases it.
Note the logged name is 'wrapper', because by the time log_call sees it, the function is already shout's wrapper.

lesson.intro:
A decorator is a function that takes another function and gives back a new one
with something added: timing, logging, changing the result. The `@name` syntax
applies it. Decorators look magical the first time, so today goes slowly and
shows what the `@` is really doing.

sections.heading: Functions are values
sections.body:
You can pass a function to another function and return functions from
functions. That's the whole foundation. Here `wrap` takes a function and
returns a new one that calls it and uppercases the result.

sections.heading: The @ syntax is just that, shorter
sections.body:
Writing `@shout` above a def is exactly the same as writing
`hello = shout(hello)` after it. The name now refers to the wrapped version.

sections.heading: Passing arguments through
sections.body:
The wrapper should accept whatever the original does. `*args` and
`**kwargs` capture anything and pass it straight along. This is the
standard shape of a decorator; copy it.

sections.heading: Decorators with arguments
sections.body:
`@repeat(3)` needs one more layer: a function that takes the argument and
returns a decorator. Three nested defs. Read it inside out: the wrapper does
the work, the decorator wraps, the outer function configures.

sections.heading: Stacking
sections.body:
Several decorators apply from the bottom up. The one closest to the def
wraps first, and the one on top wraps that.

watch_out: Forgetting `return wrapper` at the end of the decorator. The decorated function becomes `None`.
Forgetting `return func(...)` inside the wrapper. The result gets swallowed.
Writing `@shout()` with brackets when `shout` takes the function directly. Only decorators with arguments use brackets.
A decorated function's `__name__` becomes 'wrapper'. `functools.wraps` fixes that; not needed for now.
